content: It is essential to evaluate the downstream consequences of either initiating treatment following a positive test result or withholding treatment after a negative test result. These consequences include the potential development of cervical cancer and associated mortality, recurrence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN 2+), adverse effects of treatment (including overtreatment), and the utilization of healthcare resources. The recommendations provided are grounded in evidence regarding the diagnostic accuracy of various screening tests, as well as the benefits and harms associated with treatment options. This guideline is primarily directed at policymakers, healthcare managers, program officers, and other professionals in the health sector who are responsible for selecting strategies for cervical cancer prevention at national, regional, and district levels. Additionally, individuals involved in reproductive healthcare programs, particularly those focused on preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as HIV/AIDS and family planning, should also refer to these guidelines. This will help them understand the development of recommendations and the critical importance of implementing evidence-based strategies to prevent cervical cancer. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies aimed at preventing cervical cancer. In addition to these recommendations, the document includes a decision-making flowchart to assist in selecting the most appropriate screen-and-treat strategy for specific settings at the program level. It also provides detailed flowcharts for implementing these strategies, including those tailored for women with negative or unknown HIV status and for women with HIV-positive status in areas with high endemic HIV infection. The document outlines the methodology used by the World Health Organization (WHO) to develop these recommendations, including the use of the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to summarize evidence profiles and evidence-to-recommendation tables for each recommendation. These resources are available online as supplemental material. The guideline also provides the scientific rationale and justification for the practical information included in the recommendations. The WHO formed a Guideline Development Group (GDG) to oversee the creation of these screen-and-treat strategies for cervical cancer prevention. This group, chaired by Joanna Cain, consisted of 17 selected members who provided expert clinical guidance throughout the process. Additionally, an External Review Group (ERG) comprising 33 professionals, including healthcare providers, pathologists, researchers, program directors, health educators, epidemiologists, public health officers, nurses, and methodologists, was established to review and provide feedback. A Methods Group (MG) from the McGRADE Centre at McMaster University, a WHO collaborating center, contributed expertise in evidence synthesis and guideline development. In February 2011, the GDG convened to discuss the questions and outcomes to be addressed in the updated guidelines. They identified 15 potential questions to guide the evidence review for screening and treatment strategies for cervical pre-cancer. These questions were prioritized through an anonymous online survey, and eight questions were retained as the basis for the screening recommendations. The GDG also developed a list of critical outcomes to consider when making decisions and recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies. These outcomes were informed by previous work conducted for the preparation of WHO guidelines on the use of cryotherapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. The evidence synthesis process involved systematic reviews of diagnostic test accuracy and treatment effects. The MG conducted extensive searches of databases such as MEDLINE and EMBASE to identify studies related to screening strategies, including comparisons of HPV testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and cytology. Observational studies with low risk of bias were included, and data were abstracted independently by two MG members. The quality of evidence was assessed using the QUADAS tool and the GRADE approach. A mathematical model was developed to calculate the benefits and harms of each screen-and-treat strategy, considering factors such as CIN 2+ prevalence, natural progression data, pooled diagnostic test accuracy results, and treatment effects and complications. The model provided estimates of the expected absolute effects on healthcare outcomes and facilitated decision-making by summarizing evidence in evidence-to-recommendation tables. In early 2012, the GDG, ERG, and MG met to discuss and finalize the recommendations. The meeting included experts from various public health and medical disciplines, ensuring a comprehensive and geographically representative approach to guideline development.
